> The best thing about being a statistician is that you get to play in everyone's backyard. - John Tukey


Tukey's quote gives a sense of why you'd want to be a statistician/data scientist. I want to unpack what it suggests about the nature of the statistician's work that's valuable, and what "good" work looks like when you're free to move between backyards. 

When all the world is wondering about the future work, it's an interesting time to consider what good data science work looks like. Amid another round of breathless forecasting about AI-assisted work, I find the most useful precedent is not the printing press or the tulip mania but something closer to home: the Big Data movement, and what it taught us about the difference between collecting answers and discovering good questions.

## The Paradox of Big Data: Demand for Data Science

In 2005 Hadoop was invented. In 2006 AWS started offering cloud compute. In 2012 Harvard Business Review declared data science the sexiest job of the 21st century. These events look precipitous, as if the work were truly new. It is not. Data science is as old as the attempt to parse insight from numeric scratching on cuneiform tablets.

Between then and now, we've added tooling, but the process of diligent analysis, transcription and communication has not changed. The tooling mattered as much as the data itself. [Scikit-learn](https://scikit-learn.org/stable/about.html) was established early in the 2000s and went from strength to strength. Python script-kids were derisively dismissed, but they inherited the future from the Excel jockeys of the 1990s. Disputes raged across blogs about Python versus R, Jupyter notebooks versus production engineering. These petty spats about tooling were an identity crisis in disguise. Who is empowered to be a data scientist?

The ambiguity of the title opened doors. I graduated in 2009 with a degree in literature and philosophy, added post-grad work in mathematical logic, and found that none of it was especially attractive to employers. But equally employers were divided in what they wanted. Traditional titles like statistician or econometrician seemed archaic and expensive, the preserve of actual experts. The world needed a cheaper, more malleable professional. The data scientist was born: you could bootstrap yourself into the role if you could signal or demonstrate expansive competence. It was a liberating time. 

### Deep and Wide Competence

Engineers talk of the mythical 10x engineer. Data scientists have their own fable: the "unicorn" who is simultaneously computer scientist, project manager, statistician and software engineer. These chimeric creatures exist, but they are not what their job descriptions would suggest.

When I think of good data scientists I don't think of a laundry list of software they clam to use, I think of accordion players. I think of the capacity to stretch across domains and go deep into any of them. This is not merely the classic T-shaped professional, with some breadth and a specialism. The ask for a data-scientist, like the statisticians before them, is to play in __everyone's backyard__. To absorb domain context and go deep where your stakeholders can't, derive insight and value, define the problem and build the solution... and then do it all over again in the next domain.

(function() {
  const bellows = document.getElementById('bellows');
  const slider = document.getElementById('stateSlider');
  const description = document.getElementById('description');
  const wideLabels = document.getElementById('wideLabels');
  const deepLabels = document.getElementById('deepLabels');
  
  const numFolds = 16;

  for (let i = 0; i < numFolds; i++) {
    const fold = document.createElement('div');
    fold.className = 'fold';
    bellows.appendChild(fold);
  }

  const folds = bellows.querySelectorAll('.fold');

  function updateWidget(val) {
    const factor = val / 100;
    const margin = 18 * (1 - factor);
    
    folds.forEach((fold) => {
      fold.style.marginLeft = `${margin}px`;
      fold.style.marginRight = `${margin}px`;
      
      if (factor > 0.5) {
        fold.style.borderColor = `hsl(${200 - (factor * 160)}, 85%, 60%)`;
      } else {
        fold.style.borderColor = `hsl(${199 + (factor * 10)}, 89%, 54%)`;
      }
    });

    wideLabels.style.opacity = 1 - (factor * 0.7);
    deepLabels.style.opacity = 0.3 + (factor * 0.7);

    wideLabels.style.transform = `scale(${1 - factor * 0.15})`;
    deepLabels.style.transform = `scale(${0.85 + factor * 0.15})`;

    if (val < 30) {
      description.innerHTML = `<span class="highlight">Wide Competence:</span> Wandering between backyards. Connecting business problems, framing metrics, and establishing data provenance.`;
    } else if (val >= 30 && val <= 70) {
      description.innerHTML = `<span class="highlight">Dynamic Synthesis:</span> Shifting fluidly between high-level strategy and low-level statistical validation.`;
    } else {
      description.innerHTML = `<span class="highlight">Deep Focus:</span> Operating in the niche. Concentrating pressure to extract truth, refine algorithms, and build foundational rigor.`;
    }
  }

  slider.addEventListener('input', (e) => {
    updateWidget(e.target.value);
  });

  updateWidget(0);
})();
</script>

The repetitive twitch of the accordion player that pulls wide, presses deep and repeats, characterises good data science. Over time, the breadth of exposure pulls the data scientist across the business and into the thorniest areas with the least well-defined answers. Reliable discovery across that range is what makes them valuable.

### Back to Big Data
The data scientist role met with varied success — some spectacular, much of it modest to negative. Everywhere, the central promise of Big Data failed.

Scaling data collection was not enough.

Fan, Han and Liu in ["Challenges of Big Data Analysis"](https://academic.oup.com/nsr/article/1/2/293/1397586?login=false) argued convincingly that the promise of high-dimensional data is overstated. Most data collection was just scaled-up convenience sampling. Convenience samples masked obvious mistakes behind misguided confidence: yes, you had a large sample size, but the sample measured the wrong things, or the analysis overstated effects as generalisable when they reflected only the available patterns. Industry adjusted. We slowly learned that relevant data was better than convenient data.

#### AI Assisted Workflows and Convenient Answers

The data scientist plays the forward scout. They work in the untested, unexamined areas of the commercial environment. In areas of low traction and inadequate data with poor oversight and investment. A good data scientist communicates this deficit and works to improve it. Much of their value sits in the discovery, and in the recommendations made under such uncertainty.

AI-assisted workflows help the data scientist discover the limits of the available data faster and build illustrative prototypes sooner. But they will rarely decline to give an answer when asked for one. The good data scientist will give the uncomfortable answer, and then a plan for how to get a better one.

## Data Science and Commercial Relevance

The accordion workflow drives an explore/exploit process whose optimisation goal is itself ill-defined. In any one project we optimise for some commercial outcome, but we're also betting that exposure will aid __goal discovery__. What to work on and why! 

The greatest commercial value of data science is not a series of automations or a model-based solution. It is a cohort of professionals whose understanding of the business is second to none — who see which levers the business has, how responsive its outcomes are to those levers, and where tight analogies hold across domains. Their judgment is gleaned through hard-won experimentation; their breadth lets them set new targets, not just hit old ones.

AI can automate the mechanical parts of this work. What it cannot automate is the frontier: shaping how the company sees success, steering it on a new course or finding relevance in the swamp of frothy AI slop.

### How to Build Environments for Relevant Data Science

The standard "ticket-taker" model of analytics management kills the accordion motion. When data science operates as a downstream service bureau fetching data for ad-hoc requests or building isolated dashboards while training models on predetermined specs, it compresses their focus and falsely assumes that leadership already knows the right questions to ask, and the right things to build.

Kenneth Stanley and Joel Lehman in [_Why Greatness Cannot Be Planned_](https://link.springer.com/book/10.1007/978-3-319-15524-1) demonstrate why strict objective-seeking fails in complex domains. Breakthroughs rarely come from marching toward a fixed target. They come from "stepping stones" and unexpected intermediate insights whose strategic value cannot be predicted from the starting line. A data team managed like a Jira assembly line is systematically blinded to these stepping stones.

What works instead:

- __Include data science at problem definition, not problem assignment.__ Position data scientists upstream, as co-authors of strategy. Before declaring a metric or launching an initiative, involve them to evaluate framing, test assumptions, and inspect data provenance.

- __Reward stepping-stone discovery over ticket velocity.__ Assess data scientists on qualitative impact: the doomed initiatives they invalidate early, the hidden levers they uncover, the clarity they bring to ambiguous spaces.

- __Give autonomy to follow anomalous signals across departmental boundaries.__ The broken logging script found while inspecting customer-support data becomes the stepping stone to a company-wide retention fix.

- __Eliminate the translation barrier.__ A forward scout's value lies in translating low-level data realities into high-level strategic direction. Every layer of filtering dilutes the signal.

- __Deliver near-term value without losing sight of strategic goals.__ Every piece of work should serve the larger conversation between the business and its data.

When leadership treats data science as a strategic peer rather than a tactical support desk, the organization stops building models for problems it doesn't fully understand. It gains a permanent strategic radar and discovers where commercial leverage actually lies.

### How to Cultivate Good Data Scientists

The environment is only one half of the equation. The accordion motion is a demanding workflow and requires robust habits of mind. The repeated stretch-and-compress requires something instills comfort with uncertainty and builds a set of reflexes you want to train.

__Cultivate discomfort with premature certainty.__ The instinct to train a model or a build dashboard before understanding the domain is strong and rewarded by ticket-based management. Resist it. The first job in any new backyard is to map what you don't know. Encourage engagement and questioning as default.

__Learn to read a business the way you read a dataset.__ Incentive structures, org charts, budget flows — these are the features of the domain model. A data scientist who understands why a team measures what it measures can spot misalignment faster than any anomaly detector. The technical work follows from this understanding, not the other way around.

__Build the habit of writing things down for people who aren't you.__ Not documentation for its own sake, but the discipline of translating a finding into a decision. If you can't write a one-paragraph recommendation that a non-technical executive would act on, you haven't finished the analysis. The accordion compresses all the way down to rigorous method and stretches all the way up to plain language. Both endpoints matter.

__Invest in statistical foundations, not just tooling.__ Tools change every few years; the logic of inference does not. A data scientist who understands why a bootstrap works will adapt to any framework. One who only knows how to call `sklearn.model_selection.cross_val_score` is stuck when the problem doesn't fit the API. Go deep enough that you can build the tool you need when no one has built it yet. This is even easier today than before, but you need to know why to build. 

__Seek lateral exposure deliberately.__ Don't wait for the org chart to send you somewhere new. Volunteer for the messy cross-functional project. Sit in on the sales review. Read the support tickets. Every domain you touch extends the range of analogies you can draw, and analogies are the primary currency of strategic insight. The accordion stretches wider each time you play in a new backyard.

These habits compound. A data scientist who practises them for five years has a qualitatively different understanding of the business than one who spent the same five years optimising models in a single vertical. The first can set targets; the second can only hit them.
